Seneca Lake Wine Trail

Stretching along the shores of Seneca Lake in New York’s Finger Lakes, the Seneca Lake Wine Trail is home to some of the region’s most celebrated wineries and unforgettable experiences. From cool-climate Rieslings and expressive reds to vineyard views, lakeside tasting rooms, and welcoming hospitality, there’s plenty to discover at every stop. But the trail is about more than wine. It’s about slowing down, exploring somewhere beautiful, meeting the people who make the wine, and experiencing the Finger Lakes one glass, one view, and one story at a time. By JULIE SPACE

Turn Ordinary Spaces Into a Wine Destination

Add the right wine storage, and an underused basement corner becomes a private tasting retreat, while a study becomes the perfect spot for a post-work pour. title: 25 Years After 9/11, the NYC Restaurant That Sat Atop the North Tower Remains an Icon
summary:
A new CNN documentary recounts the rise and fall of the legendary World Trade Center restaurant, Windows on the World.

The post 25 Years After 9/11, the NYC Restaurant That Sat Atop the North Tower Remains an Icon appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
This year marks 25 years since the September 11 attacks and a new CNN documentary recounts the rise and fall of the iconic restaurant in the World Trade Center. Premiering on September 7, Top of the World commemorates Windows on the World, perched on the 106th and 107th floors of the North Tower, and its destruction in 2001. The 40-minute film features firsthand accounts from staff members including day-one wine director Kevin Zraly, hostess Nathalie Tolentino, prep cook Sekou Siby, and fine-dining chef—and native New Yorker—Michael Lomonaco.

Top of the World charts the restaurant’s origins: Windows on the World opened in 1976 and was conceived as a marketing effort, a way to humanize the newly built Twin Towers. The Port Authority, the operators of the Towers, turned to legendary restaurateur Joe Baum of Tavern on the Green in Central Park and The Rainbow Room at Rockefeller Plaza, who was determined to make Windows on the World iconic from opening day. 

And it was.

Originally designed by the architect Warren Platner, it was a symbol of American optimism spread out over two floors and 50,000 square feet. Wherever you sat, you had a view of Manhattan below. Everything and everyone, from the patrons who dined there to the logo illustrated by Milton Glaser, was glamorous and stylish. Dinner was a spectacle and the staff uniforms were costumes for the sky-high stage. James Beard created the food menu, which was accompanied by the biggest wine list New York City had ever seen. New York magazine deemed it “the most spectacular restaurant in the world” and Windows went on to become the highest-grossing restaurant in the country. 

“Baum really was a visionary in so many ways,” Chef Michael Lomonaco tells Wine Enthusiast. “To put a restaurant on top of a building like that was unheard of. There weren’t a lot of buildings that had restaurants on higher floors—anywhere.” 

Lomonaco says what made Windows on the World so distinct was its massive space, the incredible views, and the genuinely warm hospitality offered by a diverse staff. He recalls the restaurant on the 106th floor and the bar on the 107th. The latter went through a few different iterations with names like The Greatest Bar on Earth and Cellar in the Sky. When Lomonaco was hired in the late ’90s, the bar became a wine-focused restaurant called Wild Blue. 

Windows on the World had something for everyone, the chef says: “You had private dining spaces, big rooms, small rooms,” Lomonaco says. “There were weddings and bar mitzvahs and corporate events there. New Year’s Eve celebrations. The bar itself seated 300 people!” 

The restaurant team came from countries all over the globe, including Peru, India, Morocco, and Côte d’Ivoire. As Lomonaco puts it, “It was like the United Nations of the restaurant world.” 

At any given time, Windows had upwards of 500 employees, including cooks, porters, and waitstaff. Because they served breakfast early in the morning and drinks after dinner at night, people worked at Windows around the clock, and there were many roles that helped operations run smoothly. “At our annual holiday party, the people who worked there would bring family members. There would be a thousand people at Windows.” 

Eventually in the 1980s, Baum gave up management of Windows, with various hotel companies co-managing it. Toward the end of that decade, as the documentary chronicles, Windows became a tourist trap. When the World Trade Center bombing happened in 1993, Windows closed for three years to renovate. Baum was asked by the Port Authority to come back for the 1996 reopening and Baum chose Lomonaco, a young star chef who had worked at 21 Club, to revamp the menu and culinary operations, and he joined the Windows staff in 1997. 

At the time of his hire as chef/director, Lomonaco says, the Windows kitchens were in need of reorganization and a new game plan. It paid off: in a New York Times review of Windows, which came out on December 31, 1997, the critic Ruth Reichl awarded the restaurant  two stars and wrote that “Lomonaco’s food at Windows was nearly worthy of the view.” The chef was very appreciative of the recognition, remembering it well nearly 30 years later. 

“We had a great run, from ’97 until the end—the heyday,” Lomonaco says. “A two-star review from the New York Times was excellent! Considering that we served 600 people a night? I was thrilled. Reichl came in during the busiest time—between Thanksgiving and Christmas—to review us. It was a highlight of my career.” 

Then came the morning of September 11: There were 79 employees and 91 guests present at Windows on the World for breakfast service during the terrorist attacks. The team had been preparing for a 25th anniversary party to be thrown in October. The wine director Kevin Zraly had pre-ordered 500 cases of a special-labeled Veuve Clicquot Yellow Label. A few bottles remain today; one is housed at the Smithsonian.

Within a week of September 11, Lomonaco and a cohort of hospitality industry leaders gathered to create Windows of Hope, a charitable organization and relief fund that raised tens of millions of dollars to support the families of Windows staffers who died in the attacks.  

Despite offers to work elsewhere in the country, Lomonaco dug in his heels and stayed in New York. Now  25 years after the attacks and 50 years since Windows opened, Lomonaco is still in New York City, at the helm of Brasserie Cognac Américain, a large splashy restaurant near Bryant Park, and continues to love what he does. Hospitality is his métier, he says, and he’s having fun looking at new projects. 

“I devoted and dedicated my life to the job that I do to honor the memory of those we lost. That’s what the last 25 years has been for me,” Lomonaco says. When he ran Porter House Bar and Grill, a restaurant in Columbus Circle, from 2005 to 2025, he employed former Windows employees. “[Windows] is a constant memory. Through the work I do, I’m able to honor my friends and colleagues.”

title: Franciacorta Is the Sparkling Wine Powerhouse We’ve Been Waiting For
summary:
Writer-at-Large Jeff Porter sits down with Laura Gatti, VP of the Consorzio Franciacorta, to talk tradition, innovation, and bubbles on the WE Podcast.

The post Franciacorta Is the Sparkling Wine Powerhouse We’ve Been Waiting For appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
This episode of the Wine Enthusiast Podcast is brought to you by the Consorzio Franciacorta.

There is a moment in every wine region’s story when reputation catches up to reality. For Franciacorta, that moment arrived, and then kept arriving, year after year. But even with that critical recognition, Franciacorta has remained a wine region that strives to push forward.

Tucked into the hills of Lombardy, south of Lake Iseo, Franciacorta has spent decades doing something quietly radical: building one of Italy’s most serious sparkling wine traditions from the ground up. The region didn’t ride the coattails of a long, storied history—it was awarded DOC status relatively recently, in 1967. Rather, it has earned its place through precision, commitment, and a stubborn belief that this particular stretch of Italian earth had something extraordinary to say.

What sets Franciacorta apart is not just what’s in the glass, but the philosophy behind it. Quality here is not a talking point; it is the organizing principle of the entire denomination. From vineyard management to extended aging requirements, every decision points in the same direction: to the land, its people, and its future. Franciacorta’s forward-thinking winemakers recognize that the wines can only be as good as the soil, vines, and ecosystem that support them, and that future generations deserve to inherit something worth keeping.

In this conversation, Laura Gatti, Vice President of the Consorzio Franciacorta, makes the case for a region that is not standing still. The evolution is deliberate, the ambition is clear, and the wines have never been more compelling.

Franciacorta has always had quality. Now it has the momentum to match.

On Franciacorta’s Unique Geography

Jeff Porter: “So, what’s really interesting about this area is… so you’re kind of in the North-Central part of Italy, and the area was carved out by glaciers moving down the Alps and, you know, big knife cuts of earth and moving down all the way. And it dug out this lake called Lago d’Iseo. The soils are morainic soils. So, think of all the rocks that come from a mountain just being piled up there. And then, there’s this little mountain at the southern edge of the appellation called Monte Orfano, or the ‘Orphan Mountain.’ And basically, think of that as all the dirt that was left after the glacier melted, and it formed its own mountain.

Italy, over time, became part of a sea, and then the sea left, and the sea came back. And so, there’s also some deposits of calcareous, like, fossils and stuff like that. But it’s mainly a morainic soil-based system—really big, like, river stones and stuff like that, good drainage. It’s really kind of a Goldilocks area for making wine.

The other thing that makes it super interesting is that it’s this confluence between the beginning of the foothills of the Alps and a Mediterranean climate, and Lago d’Iseo is kind of the linchpin to all that. You know, it’s a big, deep, deep lake. At some parts of the lake, it’s a thousand feet deep, and so what that allows it to do is be a heat trap. So, the heat goes into the water and doesn’t necessarily stay around the land. It has these really beautiful diurnal shifts, you know, the temperature between day and night. Well, it’ll be warm during the day—it’ll be, like, Mediterranean climate during the day, and then the evening will be cool and alpine, and you get the winds coming down from the mountain. It’s the confluence of the Mediterranean meeting the Alps, which creates a really special place to get ripe grapes, but still maintain that acidity you need for sparkling wine.”

On When and Where to Enjoy Franciacorta

Laura Gatti: “You know, in Italy, some of the most memorable meals aren’t the formal ones. Sunday lunches with family, dinners that start at eight and somehow finish after midnight, or even a simple plate of pasta shared with friends on a Wednesday evening. That’s exactly where I see Franciacorta. Of course, it’s wonderful for celebrations, but I think its real strength is making ordinary moments feel, let’s say, a little bit more special.”

On What Daily Life Looks Like in Franciacorta

LG: “One of the things I love most about Franciacorta is that nobody seems to be in a hurry. So, you can wake up surrounded by vineyards, maybe you spend the morning cycling through the hills, and then visit a winery where the person pouring your wine is often the same person whose family has been making it for generations. It’s about local food, conversation, and taking your time.

Just 10 minutes away, there’s our Lago d’Iseo, one of the hidden gems, where people can walk along the waterfront, take a boat to Monte Isola, or simply enjoy the view with another glass of wine. It’s one of those wine regions where you can slow down, meet the producer personally and understand how deep wine is connected with the landscape.”

On What Sets Franciacorta Sparkling Apart

LG: “I think that what makes Franciacorta unique is the philosophy. Long before you taste it, there’s an extraordinary amount of care that goes into making it. From the work in the vineyards to the strict production rules that govern the denomination, every step is designed with quality over speed.

Franciacorta is made exclusively using the traditional method, where the second fermentation takes place in the bottle and the wines spend a long time aging on their lees. Nothing is rushed. Over the years, the denomination has chosen to adopt some of the most rigorous production standards in the world of sparkling wine… the belief has always been that excellence comes from attention to detail, consistency, and respect for the territory.

So if you’re standing in a wine shop wondering what makes Franciacorta different, you are choosing a wine that was never designed to be the quickest to make.”

On Gatti’s Hopes for Franciacorta’s Future

LG: “What excites me is that we are continuing to evolve without losing our identity. That’s very important. Our producers are investing heavily in biodiversity, research, and vineyard management. They are constantly asking how they can improve quality while protecting the landscape for future generations. At the same time, Franciacorta is becoming increasingly recognized around the world. Growing while remaining authentic is probably our biggest challenge and also our greatest opportunity.”

The Guests

Laura Gatti is Vice President of the Franciacorta Consortium and co-owner of one of the region’s most acclaimed wineries. An oenologist by training and a passionate ambassador of Franciacorta, she combines deep technical expertise with a strong commitment to promoting the identity, quality, and sustainability of the territory. Within the Consortium’s Board of Directors, she also serves as the councillor responsible for communication, helping to shape and strengthen Franciacorta’s voice, positioning, and reputation in Italy and international markets. Through her work in both vineyard and winery management, as well as her institutional role, she has contributed significantly to the growth and recognition of Franciacorta as one of the world’s leading sparkling wine regions. Her experience offers valuable insights into the evolution of premium sparkling wine, the importance of terroir, and the opportunities and challenges facing contemporary wine production.

So, Franciacorta is a wine region that is about 90-ish miles northeast of Milano. So, if you’re in Milan, you can hop a train, drive a car. It’s kind of like the same distance time-wise between like San Francisco and Napa Valley.

and so you’re on this really beautiful lake called Lago d’Iseo, and the wine region is centered kind of around the eastern and southern edge of that lake. And Franciacorta is specifically a sparkling wine region made in what here in Italy we call the Metodo Classico style. So that’s the secondary fermentation that takes place in the bottle And it’s a premier wine region for Italy. The Italians love it, they drink most of it that’s made. I don’t know if you’re familiar. Those who are from the south, like I am, there’s an ice cream called Bluebell ice cream, and their tagline was, “We eat all we can and then we sell the rest,” and that’s kinda how I think Italy treats Franciacorta.

JA

Well, that’s beautiful. Now I want ice cream. So about the region itself. I mean, tell me about the climate, the soils, geography. What sets this place apart?

JP

So what’s really interesting about this area is it’s this… so you’re kind of in the north central part of Italy, and the area was carved out by glaciers moving down the Alps and just, you know, big knife cuts of earth and moving this earth down all the way. And it dug out this lake called Lago d’Iseo. The soils are moranic soils. So think of all the rocks that come from a mountain just being piled up there. And then there’s this little mountain at the southern edge of the appellation called Monte Orfano or the Orphan Mountain. And basically, think of that as all the dirt that was just left after the glacier melted and it formed its own mountain. And then Italy over time became part of a sea, and then the sea left and the sea came back. And so there’s also some deposits of like calcareous, like fossils and stuff like that. But it’s mainly a moranic soil-based system, really big, like river stones and stuff like that, good drainage. It’s really kind of a Goldilocks area for making wine.

The other thing that makes it super interesting is that it’s this confluence between the beginning of the foothills of the Alps and a Mediterranean climate, and Lago d’Iseo is kind of the linchpin to all that. You know, it’s a big, deep, deep lake. At some parts of the lake, it’s a thousand feet deep, and so what that allows it to do is be a heat trap. So the heat goes into the water and doesn’t necessarily stay around the land. So it has these really beautiful diurnal shifts, you know, the temperature between day and night. Well, it’ll be warm during the day. It’ll be like Mediterranean climate during the day. And then the evening it’ll be cool and alpine. And you get the winds coming down from the mountain. So you get this really, it’s the confluence of the Mediterranean meeting the Alps, which creates a really special place to get ripe grapes, but still maintain that acidity you need for sparkling wine.

JA

Wow. So speaking of grapes, what grape varieties are we talking about here that go into Franchicorda?

JP

Okay, so think of the classic grapes you think of with the most famous sparkling wines. So you’ve got Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, but then also you’ve got Pinot Bianco, and then up to 10% of some of the wines is this local ancient grape called Erbamat. And Erbamat was actually added to the disciplinare, the rules only in 2019. but that little grape in itself is basically there as a, you know, respect towards tradition and the history, but it was recently kind of rediscovered.

But it’s you know, people know Pinot Noir, they know Chardonnay. Pinot Bianco is kind of like in the family, obviously, of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. and then Erbamat is this really bright, acidic, vibrant, energetic grape that kind of adds a little more verve to the wine.

JA

You know, talking about Italian sparkling wine, what separates Franciacorta from, you know, a Moscato or a Lambrusco?

JP

So Franciacorta, again, is… those two wines are generally made, Moscato’s made usually in the Charmat method, and same with Lambrusco. Lambrusco can also do something called rifermentato, or like kind of a petnat style. Whereas Franciacorta is made, you know, the first fermentation could be in steel or in wood, and then they put the wine in the bottle that you get at the store. They put a little more sugar and a little… and it’s some yeast, the liqueur de tirage is what the French call it, and then cap it off, and that starts the secondary fermentation in bottle. And so the pressure’s, the majority of Franciacorta is at six atmospheres, so that classic spumanti pressure. And then they have another, the cool thing, another separation with Franciacorta, they have another category called Satèn, which is a maximum of five atmospheres in it. So it’s a little less bubbly, and it’s got this, kind of more hints its name, that kind of Satin-like palette profile, really, really elegant. And they produce rosé, Blanc de Blanc, Blanc de Noir. there’s Riserva, there’s Saten.

So there’s a whole lot of different things you can do and play around with Franciacorta. And the other cool thing is the minimum aging for Franciacorta is longer than anywhere else in the world. So for the non-vintage, it has to be 18 months on the lees or sur-lie before it can even be released. So they started the region in the late sixties, I think it was ‘67, and the whole idea was to go for quality. And there’s no shortcuts in this region. And it’s relatively small in comparison to other wine regions across the globe.

JA

So, you are our, Wine Enthusiast’s dedicated Franciacorta reviewer. When you’re tasting a bottle and reviewing it, what characteristics are you looking for?

JP

You know, depending on the category, so if it’s non vintage versus vintage or riserva. So on the non vintage wines, you know, I’m looking for vibrancy, I’m looking for the aromatics to match, you know, the blend, be it Pinot Noir… so Pinot Noir might have a little more fruit character, Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, a little more green, lemon. I love to get some of that yeasty characteristic. So you can have it like, sometimes we call it brioche or fresh baked bread, and then on the palate, a richness, a creaminess, but with really, really vibrant acidity, that so with every sip I take, my mouth is refreshed so I can take another sip immediately.

JA

Fascinating. Jeff, thank you so much. I can’t wait to hear your conversation.

JP

Thank you very much.

…

Laura Gatti, ciao. Welcome to the Wine Enthusiast Podcast. We’re super excited to have you today. I know you’re in the middle of harvest, so we appreciate taking the time to talk to us about Franciacorta.

Laura Gatti

It’s my pleasure. Thank you very much for having me.

JP

No, no, my pleasure. I drink bottles of Franciacorta annually. My wife, it’s one of her favorite wines, not just from Italy, but anywhere in the world. So I’m excited to talk about it with you and get to learn more together. We’ll jump right into this. If someone’s never tasted Franciacorta before, what do you hope they experience in that first glass?

LG

Well, I always love watching someone’s reaction when they taste Franciacorta for the first time. There is usually a brief moment of surprise. People expect bubbles and freshness, and they certainly find those, but when they discover something else, the bubbles are incredibly fine, almost creamy, and suddenly they realize they are not simply drinking a sparkling wine. They are drinking a wine with real depth. What I hope they experience… I hope that first sip makes them pour another glass or maybe even start planning a trip to the region.

JP

I couldn’t agree more and and I think the moment your lips first get that hit of Franciacorta, it’s like the light bulb goes on. It’s a—

LG

Yep.

JP

It’s a unique, beautiful experience of sparkling wine. And so that leads us to, like, sparkling wine in general. Most people think of it… it’s reserved for celebrations. And I’ve spent my entire career being like ‘it’s not just for one thing,’ but how is Franciacorta meant to be enjoyed? And are we missing any part of the story?

LG

Yeah, you’re right, You know, in Italy, some of the most memorable meals aren’t the formal ones. Sunday lunches with family, dinners that start at eight and somehow finish after midnight. Or even a simple plate of pasta shared with friends on a Wednesday evening. That’s exactly where I see Franciacorta. Of course, it’s wonderful for celebrations, but I think its real strength is making ordinary moments feel, let’s say, a little bit more special.

JP

A hundred percent. I think that that’s kind of how I live my life. Sparkling wine is one of my favorite things in the world. And I love, I don’t know, I mean, I imagine you do this in your region too, is doing an entire meal, course one to the last course with Franciacorta. And I think more people should do that. You know, it’s a really beautiful experience. So you live and work in Franciacorta. What does a typical weekend look like in Franciacorta for you?

LG

One of the things I love most about Franciacorta is that nobody seems to be in a hurry. So you can wake up surrounded by vineyards, maybe you spend the morning cycling through the hills, and then visit a winery where the person pouring your wine is often the same person whose family has been making it for generations.

It’s about local food, conversation, and taking your time. Just 10 minutes away, there’s our Lago d’Iseo, one of the hidden gems, where people can walk along the waterfront and take a boat to Monte Isola or simply enjoy the view with another glass of wine.

… It’s one of those wine regions where you can slow down, meet the producer personally and understand how deep wine is connected with the landscape.

JP

I mean, I’ve been lucky enough to visit Franciacorta many times and it truly is a beautiful, seminal wine region in the world. It’s… you’re so lucky to live there. Lago d’Iseo is a special place.

So if I handed you a bottle right now and I said, Okay, Laura, show me three completely different occasions to enjoy this bottle of Franciacorta, what would they be?

LG

The first is easy, a blanket by Lago d’Iseo, some local cheese, fresh bread, a few close friends and… no rush.

And the second one would be a Michelin-starred dinner where every course is paired with a different expression of Franciacorta from Brut to Saten to Rosé and finally reaching a Riserva. That’s where people really discover how versatile these wines are. And the third one… probably at home, dinner cooking, music in the background, my family around the table.

JP

Those are the evenings you need to make sure you have more than one bottle cold in the fridge.

LG

Yeah, absolutely. At least one.

JP

Yeah. It goes too fast. Exactly.

You know, most people think that sparkling wine, and we talked about this a little bit before, that it belongs at the beginning of the meal. How would you build a day or an entire dinner around the different Franciacorta?

LG

One of the characteristics I appreciate most about Franciacorta is that the denomination offers several different styles. So each has its own personality, which makes it surprisingly easy to pair an entire menu using only Franciacorta. For sure, I’d start with a Brut as an aperitif alongside light bites. Then I’d move to a Satèn with a creamy risotto or a delicate fish. You know, Satèn has such a beautiful silky texture that it almost melts into the dish.

For the main course, perhaps a millesimato or a riserva with roasted poultry. One of the biggest surprises for many people is that Franciacorta – it’s a wine that comfortably sits at the table from the first to the last course.

JP

And I think more people need to, like, really think about having an entire meal of just Franciacorta because it is such an experience because it’s tactile, aromatic, textural, which is tactile also, but the bubbles, the depth, the richness—

LG

Yeah, the freshness also. 

JP

Exactly. Your palate never feels fatigued ever throughout the meal.

LG

You are perfectly right. I perfectly agree.

JP

I… let’s let’s do this. I’m ready.

LG

Certainly, haha.

JP

And speaking of, like, pairing food and wine together, what’s the most surprising food pairing you’ve ever had with Franciacorta?

LG

It’s a strange answer but probably fried chicken. I know it sounds unexpected but it’s fantastic. The bubble cleans the palate, the acidity balances… Another pairing I love is sushi, especially sashimi because Franciacorta enhances the delicacy of the fish without overwhelming it.

And… why not? One of the most popular Italian food, a pizza, a simple pizza that perfectly pairs with the different kinds of Franciacorta.

JP

You’ve got me, my mouth is watering. I want that bucket of fried chicken and a bottle right now.

Now, talking about the consumer being in a wine shop, and you know, when you, specifically in the States, when you’re at a wine shop or a grocery store and you’re looking at the shelf, there can be a lot of options, specifically for sparkling wine. What makes Franciacorta a unique choice? Not necessarily better, but just different.

LG

I think that what makes Franciacorta unique is the philosophy. Long before you taste it, there’s an extraordinary amount of care that goes into making it. From the work in the vineyards to the strict production rules that govern the denomination, every step is designed with quality over speed.

Franciacorta is made exclusively using the traditional method where the second fermentation takes place in the bottle and the wines spend a long time aging on their lees. Nothing is rushed. Over the years, the denomination has chosen to adopt some of the most rigorous production standards in the world of sparkling wine… the belief has always been that excellence comes from attention to details, consistency, and respect for the territory.

So if you’re standing in a wine shop wondering what makes Franciacorta different, you are choosing a wine that was never designed to be the quickest to make.

JP

I love that, a hundred percent.

So, you know, following that, you talked about the strict rules that are in place to make Franciacorta Franciacorta, and that it’s a wine that takes time. I’ve read that it has some of the longest aging before it can be released, even for the classic brut. What are those time periods that we’re looking at that you have to hold on to your wine before I even get to see it?

LG

Yeah, exactly. You’re perfectly right. The brut non-vintage must be aged at least 18 months before the disgorgement. And this is the longest time of aging for a non-vintage in the world of sparkling, like with traditional method. And we are very proud to have these strict rules because altogether we strictly work in the direction of making quality 360 degrees, starting from the vineyards.

So—how we plant our vines, how we follow the season to be able to arrive at the harvest time with grapes in perfect condition. And then we have to take care of this heritage at the cellar. Press the grapes with the entire bunches to be able to separate the different quality of juice…  First quality, second and third. And first fermentation and then bottling in spring after harvest, for second fermentation and aging on leaves. 18 months minimum for a non-vintage, 30 for a vintage, and 60 months minimum for a riserva. So, a long time, that means respect for the heritage and give to the wine the possibility to express their nature and their characteristics.

JP

Right. And I think that’s an amazing choice that you have all made as producers because that’s a long time in your cellar before you can sell the wine and you’re holding it and you’re holding it for us.

LG

Yeah, but it’s our pleasure. I mean, this is the purpose of our job, so we have to guarantee high quality. So we work with this target and the time is part of this quality. So starting from the vineyards, every step is followed to be able to bring from every harvest—that is, all the time, different from the year before, and from the year we will have to see. And we have to give to every vintage a proper identity. Consumers must find this love, this passion, this patience, this time and the territory in every glass. So this is our mission.

JP

It is very impressive and we’re lucky that you guys decided to do that. But taking a turn, I, you know, consumers, you know, we’re in this interesting time in wine right now, and consumers are more adventurous, they have more information than they’ve ever had about wine.

If someone wanted to start exploring the region, you know, how and where should they begin? And is there a style or expression that best introduces the personality of Franciacorta to the novice?

LG

I’d always suggest starting visiting the region itself. So walk around the vineyards, meet the producers, visit the cellar, have lunch in one of the local restaurants. Wine always tastes better when you understand where it comes from.

As for the style, I recommend beginning with a classic brut. It expresses the essence of Franciacorta beautifully, and then naturally invites to explore the Saten, Rosé and eventually the older Vintage and riserva.

JP

And Laura, you know, we’ve talked about Saten a few different times in this conversation, and it’s one of the most unique in the world of sparkling wine. Can you just talk about a little bit, talk about how it’s a little different than the rest of the Franciacorta and where… ’cause I find Saten to be one of the most beautiful, interesting expressions of sparkling wine in the world because it’s unique within its own self.

LG

Yeah, and Franciacorta Saten is unique for Franciacorta and for sparkling wine, generally speaking. Saten basically has three rules that make this wine different from the others, that makes this style unique. It must be a blanc de blanc, so no pinot noir allowed. It must be a brut, about sugar dosage. And saten has less bubbles compared to the other Franciacorta. So, during secondary fermentation, we can reach up to four and a half, five atmospheres instead of six. So lower pressure means a lower amount of bubbles. The final result, like the name suggests, is a silky taste. Elegance probably is the best word to describe this wine. That’s why also it can be easily paired with a wide range of food and at the same time, very different palates.

I mean, if someone wants to approach for the first time to Franciacorta, the Brut is the wine you can use to open the door. And once you step in, Saten is absolutely worth to be tried, to be tasted. So the elegance, even for people that are not so… usual consumer of bubbles, this is the best way to fall in love with our wines and our region.

JP

I’m a big—I love Saten. I highly recommend it to everybody listening. What excites you most about where Franciacorta is headed over the next decade?

LG

What excites me is that we are continuing to evolve without losing our identity. That’s very important. Our producers are investing heavily in biodiversity, research, and vineyard management. They are constantly asking how they can improve quality while protecting the landscape for future generations. At the same time, Franciacorta is becoming increasingly recognized around the world. Growing while remaining authentic is probably our biggest challenge and also our greatest opportunity.

JP

What exactly are you working on in terms of biodiversity within the region itself?

LG

We are experimenting in cooperation with six universities in Italy and also outside Italy, a lot of different… We are studying, again, the soils, we are checking and monitoring all the insects. Yeah, it’s quite the project and it will take place for the next three and four years because it takes time to produce our wines and at the same time it takes time to study, to develop, to do research. But the main purpose behind all the experiments we are doing or the research we are doing is to preserve the heritage of Franciacorta for the next generation to be ready, to be prepared to face the weather changing, because we don’t want to lose the identity and the style of the region and we have to be careful, to be prepared. So it takes a long time for everything, even to study. So we have to start to be, in the near future, ready to face everything that can happen and to know, deeply, the changing, not only style, on the taste of the wine, on the weather…. But also to know, even more than now, everything that works around the wine world. So biodiversity is one of the steps. Then also we are studying the possibility of using water, of, yeah, it’s… It’s a new project, so a lot to do, a lot of new things to work on.

JP

I mean, I think, you know, for those listening too, why it’s really important, the consortium and its members, which are all the producers who belong to the consortium, are investing their time and their energy and their money into doing this research so they can continue their legacy. They can continue the ideas that they have and the values that they have, which is like, you know, which is an amazing project and I look forward to learning more next time I come visit.

And one other kind of technical question for those that don’t know Franciacorta as a region: You know, if you put in your mind’s eye, if you’re in Milan, you go about ninety miles northeast, you come to Lago d’Iseo, you come to, like, this main city called Ubrosco, right? Ibresco.

LG

Erbusco is where the consortium is. And that’s 19 villages all around, part of Franciacorta wine region.

JP

There we go, thank you. And how many hectares about is the region as a whole?

LG

Vineyards that are producing grapes… now are 3,500. In the last few years, we’ve noticed an increase of the surface planted. So in the next three, four years, we will reach around 4,000.

JP

So just for our listeners in the United States, so three thousand five hundred hectares is about eight thousand six hundred and acres of land—

LG

Acres, yeah.

JP

Which, when you put in the context of wine, is very, very small. It is not a lot of land. So just to make sure, for everybody listening, that Franciacorta is a really small wine appellation in the greater idea of wine, as other regions throughout the world, it’s very, very small.

LG

Yeah, the total production… the current production is 20 million bottles per year. Some wineries are producing, alone, 20 million. We are a tiny, tiny wine region, but again, focused in high quality. And yeah, we are working every day to do it better.

JP

Well, we greatly appreciate that for you. So, if you could convince every wine lover to change just one habit about sparkling wine, what would it be?

LG

I’ll tell them to stop saving it. Simply. Don’t wait for New Year’s Eve, don’t wait for an anniversary. Open the bottle on a Tuesday, serve it with takeaway sushi, bring it to a barbecue or share with neighbors.

JP

100%. The beauty of wine is it creates moments of community and sharing and conviviality. And that’s why it’s so important.

LG

Yeah.

JP

Awesome. Well, thank you very, very much, Laura. I know you’re super busy. I’m gonna ask one more question. I apologize. You’re in the middle of harvest.

LG

Yeah.

JP

How’s it going?

LG

Let’s say… it’s going well. It’s not an easy season and we are harvesting a little bit in advance compared to the regular period because we have had quite hot temperatures in the last couple of weeks. The grapes are perfectly ripened and the weather is… the sun is shining. So we are working very fast. I think in a couple of weeks everything will be done and all the new wines will be fermenting in the cellars. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are showing perfectly and we expect good quality, not big quantity because unfortunately we have had a hail storm in springtime, early springtime, so the quantity is below the average but we expect very good quality and for this season, very strong personality.

JP

In a minimum of eighteen months we’ll get to see what the brut looks like, with a little bit of 2026 in it.

LG

We will find out on the glass.

JP

Exactly. Well Laura, thank you very, very much. Good luck with the rest of harvest. We greatly appreciate your time and it was a lot of fun speaking about this beautiful wine region of Franciacorta with you.

LG

Thanks for having me. Thanks for talking about Franciacorta. Have a nice summer with a glass of Franciacorta in your hands. Grazie, ciao!

JP

Assolutamente, grazie mille. Ciao.

You know, Laura gave us a lot of good insight into Franciacorta, and my favorite take is: bubbles with fried chicken or on a Tuesday night is the way you can level up your life with Franciacorta. Let us know what you think. You can email us your comments and questions at podcast@wineenthusiast.com. And remember, you can subscribe to this podcast on Apple, Spotify, and anywhere else you listen to your favorite shows. You can also go to wineenthusiast.com/podcast for more episodes and transcripts.

I’m Jeff Porter and thanks for listening.

title: Tariffs Hurt the Wine Industry. Did the Refunds Stop the Bleeding?
summary:
After years of back-and-forth tariff headaches, billions of dollars are back in importer pockets. Are there more worries to come?

The post Tariffs Hurt the Wine Industry. Did the Refunds Stop the Bleeding? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • In February, the Supreme Court ruled past tariffs illegal, forcing the U.S. government to refund $166 billion to importers.
  • Importers report that the new digital refund system is surprisingly smooth, despite a few minor delays.
  • Companies are saving their refund cash as a safety net rather than lowering prices for consumers.

This February, after almost two years of headaches caused by President Donald Trump’s global trade war, some good news arrived for American importers and international producers: the United States Supreme Court ruled that the tariffs put in place by the Trump administration were illegal, and the government must return the payments they raked in—a sum totaling $166 billion.

This means that any importer who paid additional tariffs on goods entering the United States from abroad is eligible to get their money back. On the whole this is good news. But after all the ups and downs of heavy-handed and mercurial tariffs, many in the wine industry expected the refund process to be a mess of red tape or another logistical nightmare for importers to manage.

In April, US Customs and Border Protection launched the Consolidated Administration and Processing of Entries (CAPE) portal through which companies can submit their requests for tariff refund claims. As of August, about $100 billion in tariff returns have been processed across industries. According to wine importers and experts who spoke to Wine Enthusiast, the refund process is going largely smoothly, to many people’s surprise, and businesses are receiving a welcome injection of cash. 

But as in all government-related bureaucracies, it hasn’t been without hassle. Distributors and importers report the ups, downs, and surprising silver linings of the tariff refund process.

The Refunds

The tariff situation has been, in short, a nightmare. After all importers have gone through with tariff rates ebbing and flowing, it’s understandable that many expected the refund process to be utter chaos. How would the system work? More importantly, would people actually get their money back? And how much? Should we be excited, they asked, or is this another headache in the tariffs race?

“Because tariff rules and rates were changing frequently, we often did not know the final tariff cost until shipments arrived,” says Andy Rieger, co-founder of J. Rieger & Co., based in Kansas City, Missouri. “As a result there is still uncertainty around what percentage of the tariffs will ultimately be refunded. Depending on final determinations, the total refund could amount to a meaningful five-figure sum for us.”

But rather unexpectedly the refunds are going well. 

“The government did a good job setting up the portal,” says Victor Schwartz, founder of New York-based wine and spirits importer VOS Selections—and one of the catalysts behind the Supreme Court case that led to the dismantling of the tariffs. “It’s very clear, and very nicely done. We expected a really hard time. Certainly the administration set us up to think that it was going to be, quote, unquote a mess, and it wasn’t. Everything is digitized.”

Andrea Nappi, the president of the National Association of Beverage Importers says, “All you need to do is include an entry number—it’s an Excel spreadsheet with one column that you upload.” However not everything has been free of mistakes or glitches, she adds: “People are getting errors and upload notifications that [the claim] didn’t go through. But on the scale that they have done it, I think overall it’s been pretty decent.” 

For the most part, these are fixable oversights or doable tasks, if time-consuming, like correcting incomplete forms or finding the right digital paperwork to fill out. People have compared it to filing taxes. Nappi says, “It’s part of working with a big company or the government.”

The Roadbumps

One of the major issues is that not everyone has received their refunds. It’s been over 90 days since the CAPE portal was launched, and some importers are still waiting for their money back. “The process appears to operate in multiple rounds tied to shipment timing, with more recent imports becoming eligible first,” says Rieger.

Any entry that was liquidated also is up for debate. Andrew Sinclair, CEO of González Byass USA, has received tariff refunds in the six figures, plus interest, but Sinclair also has a dozen entries that are unresolved, all liquidated and currently under protest. As an importer he had to make decisions: Is the cost and time of battling potential refunds worth it? “You just make a calculation,” Sinclair says. “What percentage of that fee is your potential refund? Does it make sense to speculate?”

Additionally, the Trump administration’s volatile tariff war is not over, and more questions continue to arise. In July, when the tariffs that the Supreme Court deemed illegal ended, Trump announced a 10% to 12.5% tariff would be imposed on imports from the US’s top 60 trade partners including the U.K., Europe, and China. 

In that same month, Trump also implemented an additional 50% tariff on certain goods from Canada, and there’s fear that the administration could extend it to other trading blocs like the European Union. What will happen with all these new tariffs, and will refunds apply in the future?

Kyle Peacock, principal of Peacock Tariff Consulting, recommends that importers use their tariff refunds strategically. “Our view is not to treat the refunds as free money to spend, but to treat it as a reserve.” Amid the seemingly-endless tariff wars, Peacock believes that the businesses in the best position to weather the next wave “won’t be the ones who spent their refund on expansion. They’ll be the ones who keep a cushion to absorb the next round.”

The Silver Linings

Through the turmoil caused by ever-changing international tariffs, there’s a productive bottom line: The refunds provided have put more cash to American businesses, which in turn allows them to be more strategic and nimble in a difficult market. 

“As an independent spirits brand, competing against multinational companies is already challenging,” Rieger says. “Our focus remains on consistency: maintaining product quality, supporting fair and sustainable pricing, and building the brand long-term rather than reacting to short-term volatility.”

Now that refunds are in place, a question is whether or not prices will soften. If the cost of wine increased to accommodate the tariff rates, will they then lower, now that the tariffs have been repealed? Sinclair has seen prices rise $2 to $4 a bottle, with lower tier wines priced around $9 feeling the most pressure. “They feel the pinch harder. Tariffs make up a disproportionate amount of value,” he says.

But unfortunately when prices rise, they rarely lower. Consider how, during the Covid-19 pandemic, prices for everything from meals at restaurants to toilet paper increased and never truly came back down to pre-2020 figures. Not only are importers wary of what’s to come, but they feel their businesses have already weathered enough.

Rather than pass the full cost of the tariffs onto distribution partners, many importers absorbed some of the hit. Sinclair, for example, increased prices 5% rather than the full 10%. He’s not sure what to anticipate next. 

“It’s just the new normal,” he says. “It’s another challenge during an unprecedented moment and uncharted waters, in terms of consumer behavior and distributor consolidation.”

title: These 23 Apple Cocktails Are Delightful for Fall—or Anytime
summary:
Forget pumpkin spice. Autumn is the season for apple-forward beverages.

The post These 23 Apple Cocktails Are Delightful for Fall—or Anytime appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
The air is getting crisper, the sun is setting earlier, and the leaves are beginning to change. You know what that means: Autumn is here—and so is apple season. 

There’s no better time than fall to enjoy the sweet fruit that’s associated in folklore with magic and divination. Meanwhile, eating apples at Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, is considered to be an omen for good luck and prosperity. 

While the apples are often baked into pies and cakes, we think one of the finest, and less expected, ways to enjoy the fruit is in a cocktail. It’s a remarkably versatile flavor. Mix in juice for a refreshing tang, try an expressive apple-based brandy, like Calvados or Applejack, or experiment with a flavorful apple liqueur. 

We rounded up 23 of our favorite recipes for apple-flavored cocktails below.

The Autumn Apple

As the name of this cocktail suggests, the Autumn Apple is a celebration of the season thanks to applejack, apple cider, and a fresh apple garnish. It’s also infused with thyme, lending it a whisper of fall herbaceousness. Batch the recipe and get ready to impress a crowd.

Slice of Pie

If the syrupy-sweet apple pie cocktail commonly found on college campus is a bit too much for you, how about a Slice of Pie? This cocktail gives us all of the fall vibes thanks to its frozen apple juice concentrate, apple brandy, and orange bitters.

Apple Cider Spritz

Is it technically a spritz or a spritzer? Who cares when it tastes this good. This apple cider spritz combines spiced apple cider syrup and whiskey with sparkling water for a refreshing treat that scratches that fall itch.

Cider Doughnut Daiquiri

Adapted from a cocktail served at the Austin bar Elementary, the cider doughnut daiquiri was inspired by bartender Jode Gayle’s memories of going to the county fair. With spiced rum, apple cider, and a cinnamon sugar rim, you’ll almost feel like you have a bucket of doughnuts in front of you.

Apple Cider Margarita

What can’t you do with a classic margarita? Its beloved tangy, sweet flavor is ideal for doctoring with the similar profile of apples. The apple cider margarita uses reposado tequila and apple cider and finishes off with a cinnamon-sugar rim.

Franconia 75

Named after a mountain in New Hampshire, the Franconia 75 is like a French 75 who moved to New England. The riff gets its Northeastern twist from maple syrup and chilled dry cider instead of the usual Champagne float.

A Farewell to Arms

Will Lee of Grey Ghost Detroit crafted this bourbon-based cocktail to warm you up on a chilly day, and its name, A Farewell to Arms, is actually a reference to wearing garments for cold weather, not the Ernest Hemingway book. Made with Laird’s apple brandy, Pedro Ximenez sherry, and Benedictine, it certainly packs a punch.

Yule Tide Toddy

Don’t let its name fool you—the Yule Tide Toddy, made with apple bitters, bourbon, and Amaro Abano, shouldn’t be reserved for Christmas. Serve it anytime you need a warming refreshment.

The Country Store

The Country Store is an Old Fashioned riff that features Laird’s Applejack in place of the classic bourbon. Lara Creasy, the bar consultant behind this recipe, likes to serve it as an aperitif.

Stone Fence Riff #1

A variation on the colonial-era tradition of spiking a hard drink with spirits, the Stone Fence Riff #1 is an apple cider cocktail dosed with rum and allspice simple syrup.

Bitter Candied Apple

Adapted from the Washington D.C. bar Boqueria, the Bitter Candied Apple boasts apple cider and Licor 42, a vanilla-infused Spanish liqueur.

The Roustabout

The Roustabout takes inspiration from the classic Manhattan and Old Fashioned but tailors them specifically for fall. The bourbon-based drink has remarkably seasonal flavors thanks to walnut liqueur and Calvados.

Spiced Cranberry Orange Wassail

If you love mulled wine and hot cider, the Spiced Cranberry Orange Wassail is for you. It’s made by simmering apple juice with oranges, cranberries, and spices like anise pods, cinnamon sticks, and fresh ginger. Top with whiskey and enjoy.

Apple Cider Sangria

All hail the endlessly adaptable Sangria, which is essentially wine fruit punch. Of course, apple would be a flavor to lean into. With this apple cider sangria, you mix apple cider with Calvados (or another apple brandy) and dry white wine.

The Group Text

This batched cocktail is a great excuse to bring your friends together and celebrate the changing season. The Group Text starts with a base of apple cider, whiskey, and ginger liqueur and is topped with sparkling wine for a refreshing lift.

The Get Up and Goji

The Get Up and Goji features vodka distilled from fresh-pressed apple cider, kombucha, mint and apple cider. 

Appletini

No—this isn’t the radioactive green, saccharine ’90s cocktail. This updated appletini is elevated by Calvados, elderflower liqueur, and apple juice.

Mi Nonie

Made with just one ounce of mezcal, the Mi Nonie’s low-abv makes it perfect for day drinking. Apple cider vinegar and honey clove syrup give a spicy tartness to pair with the smoky depth.

Pink Lady

A classic egg white cocktail, the frothy and sweet Pink Lady gets its hue from grenadine and its flavors from gin, applejack, and lemon juice. 

Brandy Slush

Known regionally as “Wisconsin Sangria,” the Brandy Slush is perfect for those early fall days when it’s just warm enough for a frozen drink. For an extra fall twist, and Great Lakes Distillery bartender Brendan Cleary’s favorite way to mix the frozen drink, use apple brandy.

Black Sands

Think of the Black Sands as another seasonal bridge: It’s slightly summery thanks to rum and fresh mint, yet autumnal courtesy of Calvados apple brandy.

Angel Face

A recipe for this Prohibition-era spirit-forward drink was found in the 1930 publication of The Savoy Cocktail Book. The Angel Face is an equal-parts drink made with Calvados, gin, and apricot brandy liqueur.

The Basement Milk Cocktail

Arosa ski hotel The Tschuggen Grand serves The Basement Milk Cocktail in its basement lounge, as its name might suggest, where it’s a rich nightcap designed to help end the evening. It’s made with cream, Frangelico, apple cider, and Calvados, among other ingredients.

title: At Sushi Nakazawa LA, All Eyes Are on the Showpiece Sake Cellar
summary:
The restaurant’s centerpiece cellar displays rare bottles from their award-winning sake list.

The post At Sushi Nakazawa LA, All Eyes Are on the Showpiece Sake Cellar appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Since opening in 2013 in New York City’s Greenwich Village, Sushi Nakazawa has been considered one of the top omakase spots in the country. Chef Daisuke Nakazawa, a former apprentice of revered sushi chef Jiro Ono (who starred in Jiro Dreams of Sushi), offers tastings of his signature Edomae-style nigiri, as well as a menu of hot and cold dishes. Beverage Director Dean Fuerth’s sake pairings are an integral part of experience. In fact, the original NYC outpost has the largest selection of sakes in the United States. For the past four years, The World of Fine Wine named it “Best Sake List, North America.” 

Due to space restrictions, most of it is hidden away in a basement. But when the team opened their third location in Los Angeles this past spring, they put those rare selections of full display in their centerpiece cellar.

The Design: Made of polished brass and double glass panes, the modern showpiece features a label-forward design that shows off the rarest bottles in the collection. “Given that sake has become such a big part of the restaurant, we really wanted to put it on display,” says Fuerth. “We wanted to showcase rarities and the access we have to incredible beverages that we’ve been able to get through our personal relationships with producers—some of which less than a handful of bottles come in the country.”

In addition to the 300 bottles that are displayed and stored on those brass shelves, this gem of a cellar holds approximately 2,000 bottles organized across 68 bins. It’s chilled to a cool 48 degrees and serves as the primary storage for the restaurant’s collection of sake, Champagne, and white wine—though the staff needed to buy four additional EuroCaves that house 200 bottles apiece to hold the rest of the wine.

The Collection: The Los Angeles location boasts 250 sakes—the largest selection in all of California—and 350 wines. (New York has 450 sakes and 700 wines.) While the sheer volume is impressive, what really sets the collection apart is the ethos from which it was built. Following his experience of developing French wine lists, Fuerth showcases sake producers and regions through various vintages and price tiers. For example, the list includes three different lineups from Nizawa Sake Brewery including its least expensive table sake “Atago No Matsu,” a classic Honjozo-style sake that contains a small addition of brewer’s alcohol to extract more flavor (for $85 a bottle), to its insanely expensive Reikyo Crystal 0. A 500-milligram bottle of the hard-to-find Junmai Daiginjo sake made from a record-breaking 0.85% rice polishing ratio goes for $17,500 apiece. These diverse offerings “show the different quality levels as well as the house style of each producer and each region,” says Fuerth.”It’s a storytelling element.”

What Makes It Special: The cellar is used to tell that story in a striking 3D display. “My favorite part of the case is the right side,” says Fuerth, where he displays a lineup of bottlings that highlight the work of celebrated master brewer Noguchi Naohiko, known as the “God of Sake Brewing.” “He worked at a few historical breweries, before he went on to open Noguchi Naohiko Sake Institute. It’s a way to talk about the list in a visual way—it vertically explores the history of where he’s worked and his influence.”

title: In This Fantasy Football League, Wine Is the Prize
summary:
Want to get your oenophile friends into football? Just add wine.

The post In This Fantasy Football League, Wine Is the Prize appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Every September, millions of people enthusiastically sign up for a fantasy football league. In this months-long game of pretend, participants role-play as owners and managers of fake football teams composed of actual players in the NFL, whose real-world performances in real-world games determine how many points are awarded to each contestant in the fantasy league. 

It is—or rather can be—a lot of fun. But very quickly after the start of each season, participants realize that they’ve accidentally adopted a second job. Suddenly there are waiver wires to monitor, injury reports to decipher, Thursday night deadlines to remember, lineup changes to make, and enough group-text notifications to make you wonder whether you’ve joined a Fortune 500 board meeting instead of a friendly football league. 

For diehard NFL fans, that’s part of the appeal. For everyone else, it’s often enough to stay on the sidelines.

As the publisher of Blood Of Gods, a magazine exploring the intersection of wine and heavy metal, I’ve come to believe that some of the most interesting communities are built where seemingly unrelated passions overlap. Wine has an uncanny ability to bring people together, but pair it with another passion—music, art, or sports—and suddenly entirely new conversations begin. 

Last season, after a few years of friendly football trash talk, my friend Jess Forster, a sommelier at Waxlight Bar à Vin in Buffalo, New York, and I started wondering if there was a way to create an NFL pool that felt less like homework and more like opening a bottle with friends. We wanted a fantasy football league for people who don’t actually want to play fantasy football.

The solution turned out to be almost embarrassingly simple. 

Instead of asking everyone to manage a fantasy roster for four months, we asked each participant to contribute a bottle of wine and make one round of predictions before Week One. That’s it. 

Once the season kicked off, there were no weekly picks to submit, no roster changes to agonize over, and no forgotten deadlines to derail your season—just football, wine, and the slow satisfaction of watching your predictions either age beautifully or spectacularly fall apart.

The result was so much fun that we immediately realized we’d stumbled onto a format worth sharing, one that could easily be replicated by anyone with a tasting group, wine club, workplace, or just a handful of friends.

Start with One Bottle

The only buy-in is a bottle of wine. 

It doesn’t have to be rare or expensive. The goal isn’t to impress anyone. It’s simply to build a prize pool that everyone would genuinely be excited to win. Some people brought dependable everyday favorites while others reached into the cellar for something they had been waiting for an excuse to open.

By kickoff, the growing collection of bottles had become an event unto itself. Familiar labels sat beside cult wines, local producers mingled with bottles from across the country, and people were already circling the wines they’d love to take home. Before anyone had earned a single point, we’d unintentionally assembled one of the most eclectic bottle shares imaginable. 

Our league included thirty participants, which meant thirty bottles of wine waiting at the finish line for our lucky winners.

Make Your Picks—Once

To keep things approachable, we built a simple Google Form that participants could complete in about five minutes. 

The form asks for each participant’s predictions for who will win the AFC and the NFC (the American Football Conference and the National Football Conference, the two major halves that make up the NFL—you know, the National Football League); who will go head-to-head in the Super Bowl; who will become the Super Bowl champion, as well as their Wild Card teams. (Sure, this takes a bit of research, but it’s easy enough to complete the form with a glass of wine in hand.) 

Once everyone clicks “submit,” the picks are locked for the season. That’s the entire commitment. Seriously.

From that point forward, all that’s left to do is watch the standings unfold. Even people who couldn’t name three quarterbacks suddenly found themselves checking division races three months into the season because, somehow, they had skin in the game.

Keep the Scoring Simple

One of the biggest lessons we learned is that simplicity wins.

It’s tempting to create elaborate scoring systems, but resisting that urge keeps the pool welcoming to casual fans.

We awarded one point for every correct division winner, one point for each correctly predicted Wild Card team, two points for each Super Bowl participant, and three points for correctly picking the eventual champion. 

One of our favorite discoveries was how little maintenance the league required. Aside from the occasional leaderboard update or check-in with the group, the season largely takes care of itself, allowing everyone to simply enjoy watching their predictions slowly rise—or collapse. There was no spreadsheet fatigue, no midseason drop-off and no one asking, “Wait…am I supposed to be doing something this week?”

Winner Takes (Most of) the Wine

Our favorite format was “winner takes most.”

With thirty bottles in the pool, first place received eighteen bottles, second place took home eight, and third place claimed the remaining four.

It struck a nice balance. The top finishers went home with an enviable haul, while spreading the prizes across three places kept more people invested until the very end.

Keep It Interesting

One thing we discovered quickly is that even though the picks never change, and most of the scoring naturally unfolds as the postseason arrives, people still enjoy having little moments of interaction throughout the season. 

Our first amendment to the league was a Best Team Name competition, roughly a third of the way into the season.

Predictably, as a group of participants that come largely from the wine world, we were incapable of resisting terrible puns. Names like Cab Sauv Your Ass, The Brutal Bruts, and a few Brettanomyces jokes made the rounds, but the eventual winner was Pfalz Start, a name that somehow managed to delight both the football crowd and the wine geeks. The winner earned two bonus points for the clever appellation after a community vote.

Later in the season, we held another vote for the bottle everyone most wanted to win. Surprisingly it became almost as competitive as football itself. In our inaugural season, the runaway favorite was a Hermann J. Wiemer Blanc de Noirs 2012 with a ten-year disgorgement. Its owner also earned two bonus points.

Neither award had anything to do with football, yet both became some of the season’s liveliest debates.

Keep the Conversation Going

Although no one had to submit anything after Week One, a few occasional updates helped keep the momentum alive.

We celebrated the participant whose improbable Super Bowl prediction suddenly looked brilliant. We commiserated with the unfortunate soul whose championship matchup was mathematically eliminated before Halloween. For your game, you might even share a leaderboard every few weeks if you feel like it.

If you really want to lean into the wine theme, have a little fun with featured games. Bills versus Ravens? Reach for Cabernet Sauvignon and prepare for controlled violence. A rainy Seahawks afternoon practically screams for Oregon Pinot Noir. Chiefs versus Eagles? Open Champagne—you’ll probably need something celebratory regardless of the outcome.

The pairings don’t have to make perfect sense. They’re conversation starters, and that’s the point.

Foster the Community

What surprised us most wasn’t how competitive the pool became. It was the wonderfully unexpected mix of people who embraced it. 

One participant had recently moved to the Northwest and, by their own admission, knew literally nothing about the NFL. They followed college football, but the pro game was another planet. So in the spirit of embracing a new home, they chose the Seahawks to go all the way. 

Months later, after Seattle won the Super Bowl, that same newcomer—and NFL newbie—came in third place, walked away with a stash of stunner bottles, and the kind of accidental bragging rights that no amount of preseason research could have guaranteed.

Friends who had never watched an entire football game suddenly found themselves following playoff scenarios. Wine professionals who disappear into harvest each autumn could still participate without having to remember weekly deadlines. Partners who normally rolled their eyes at fantasy football suddenly had a reason to cheer on Sunday afternoons.

As Forster puts it, “I think humans in general want and sometimes even ache for community. When you can connect with other wine enthusiasts or professionals through the lens of sports or music or other topics, it’s so fun.” 

The format also remains intentionally low lift, allowing people to be as involved—or uninvolved—as they want to be throughout the season.

This isn’t just a football pool. Football is simply the framework. It could be literally anything else—basketball, Formula 1, RuPaul’s Drag Race. 

The real reward is creating another reason for people to gather, laugh, exchange a little friendly trash talk, and stay connected throughout a season, particularly the fall and winter. It’s a reminder that wine has always been at its best when it brings people together, and that sometimes all it takes is another shared passion to make that happen.

If your tasting group, office, or family has been looking for a new tradition this fall, consider this fantasy-football-league-but-with-wine your blueprint. Collect a few bottles, pour a glass, lock in your picks before Week One, and let the season do the rest. 

You might walk away with eighteen bottles of wine or zero. But if our experience is any indication, you’ll also walk away with a tradition everyone is already looking forward to repeating before the next kickoff.

title: Wine Grapes Are Thriving In One of the Driest Places On Earth
summary:
Over the last two decades, winemakers have been flocking to Chile’s Atacama Desert for its distinct and vibrant character.

The post Wine Grapes Are Thriving In One of the Driest Places On Earth appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
When you step off the plane in Copiapó, the gateway to Chile‘s Atacama region, the vast, dusty landscape makes you wonder how a single vine could survive here—let alone thrive. 

The answer lies in the transverse valleys that stretch from the Andes Mountains to the Pacific Ocean, flourishing even alongside and within the Atacama, the world’s driest non-polar desert. Cooling coastal breezes, rivers, and temperature shifts at higher altitudes make viticulture possible in this seemingly inhospitable landscape. 

Since the 16th century, locals in the northern Huasco, Elqui, and Limarí Valleys have cultivated grapes primarily for Pisco. Over the last two decades, however, wine producers have begun exploring this area, known as Norte Verde (which translates to Green North).

Wines made here are vibrant and fresh, with a distinct character that sets them apart from those of Chile’s central valleys. This isn’t a passing trend but an emerging expression of Chilean wine built on a shared commitment to premium, low-intervention, terroir-driven winemaking.

Huasco Valley: Freshness in the Atacama Desert

In 2010, Ventisquero Wine Estates planted its first vines in the Huasco Valley, a remote region on the southern border of the Atacama Desert where few producers had previously ventured. 

“Even there, in the driest desert on earth, the Pacific Ocean and the Camanchaca fog bring freshness and balance to the vineyards,” says Horacio Fuentes, Ventisquero’s export director.

The estate’s vines grow just 13 miles from the coast, and despite its location, the valley is not hot. Thanks to the sea, average annual temperatures range from 62°F to 66°F, and the Huasco River ensures water is readily available, too.

The range of soils includes sandy loam and clay with varying salt content, but it’s the limestone that defines the valley’s character.

“What surprises people most about these wines is not their power, but their elegance and freshness,” Fuentes says. “You get purity, tension, minerality, and natural acidity.” 

Ventisquero’s goal is to make wine that reflects its origin. Winemakers achieve that end with a low-intervention approach, employing native yeast and aging in untoasted foudres or cement eggs, and avoiding filtering before bottling.

The Elqui Valley: Vineyards that Scrape the Stars

At the edge of the Atacama Desert, the picturesque Elqui Valley is renowned for its Pisco production. But it’s also an emerging region for delicious wines with dramatic tension.

Agriculture in Elqui follows the Turbio River from the Andes Mountains to the Pacific Ocean. Wine producers tend to prefer higher elevation areas of over 7,000 feet, where the vines grow on granite, clay, and silt soils, and diurnal temperature shifts caused by high altitude and clear skies allow the grapes to fully mature.

“Making mountain wine limits you in many ways, but the grape quality is unique,” says Viñedos de Alcohuaz winemaker Rosario Fillol. “You get intense concentration, excellent natural acidity, and vibrancy.” Here, winemakers celebrate the incredibly distinct landscape, and are genuinely committed to terroir and a clear regional identity.

“Producers in the Norte Verde respect the land and work with less conventional winemaking approaches that reflect the region in the glass,” adds Fillol. 

Her team stomps grapes barefoot in granite lagares made from mountain rocks, seeking a softer extraction for an enhanced tannic structure. They also utilize concrete eggs and amphorae to allow micro-oxygenation without imparting flavors, so the Elqui character shines through.

Limarí Valley: The Power of Limestone and Ocean Influence

The Limarí valley is in the Coquimbo region next to the Atacama, and its top vineyards are located near the Pacific Ocean. This coastal influence lowers temperatures, reduces sunlight, and brings morning fog and higher humidity. As a result, grapes here ripen slowly, which is crucial for delicate varieties like Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

But growing vines in Limarí is not easy. In some areas, that coastal influence can complicate things, leaving plants needing protection from the strong ocean breezes, and producers like Tabali having to blend aquifer water with river water to reduce salinity before irrigating.

Chardonnay, in particular, greatly benefits from Limarí’s terroir. Utilizing the region’s limestone soils, which provide wines with exquisite vibrancy, winemakers can maximize the grape’s unique flavor profile.

“Limarí Chardonnay tends to show a more restrained aromatic profile, less intense and less fruity, with a distinct flavor expression,” says Felipe Müller, CEO and chief winemaker at Tabali. The wines are “sometimes slightly saline, with a chemical balance that sets it apart from other cool-climate regions in Chile.” 

Seeing the success of Limarí’s wines, powerhouse labels like Santa Rita and Amelia (Concha y Toro) have started to source grapes and produce wines in the region. These bottlings can be bright and flinty or focused and elegant, but all express the Valley’s signature mineral characteristics.

Additionally, a growing focus on premium wines has been key in establishing the northern valleys as a quality wine region.

“There are few wineries in this area, and the overall quality level is significantly higher compared to the Central Valley and other regions with many producers,” says Müller. “This has been crucial in quickly establishing many of these wines among Chile’s top offerings.” 

In a relatively short time, wines from Huasco, Elqui, and Limarí have developed strong identities that express and surpass the extreme climate where the vines grow. Winemaking in Chile has never been easy—but it’s never been more exciting, either.

title: Why ‘Quality Over Quantity’ Is Good for the Wine Industry
summary:
Consumption may be down, but open-mindedness and willingness to spend is up.

The post Why ‘Quality Over Quantity’ Is Good for the Wine Industry appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Chris Liu believes that there’s a bright side to shorter bar tabs. 

“People are drinking less in terms of quantity, but I find them more discerning in terms of quality,” says the beverage director of Bloomsday, a wine bar and restaurant in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. “They’re very intentional about what they buy.”

The practice extends beyond Bloomsday’s barstools. People of all ages, appetites, and tax brackets are recalibrating their consumption habits and redefining value at the bar and bottle shop—and it could have a big impact on wine. Whether that’s a positive development depends on your outlook and how much time we all have. 

As countless headlines and Reddit threads will tell you, modern wine businesses face an array of evolving social, economic, and environmental challenges. But the drink-less-but-better movement isn’t an existential threat. It’s proof that many people who are cutting back are still interested in wine and eager to make the most out of every glass or bottle they try. 

Armchair analysts who bemoan generational shifts and elegize consumption data tend to ignore this crucial detail: People who are drinking wine are doing so more skillfully and thoughtfully than ever before. That’s not a silver lining so much as lightning in a bottle. The only question is whether there’s enough time for it to ignite.

Curiosity Takes Center Stage

“There’s been a steady evolution in the way people drink wine,” says Jamie Ritchie, the managing director of international auctions at Berry Bros. & Rudd in Washington, D.C. In previous decades, many collectors would purchase multiple cases from known regions or producers without investigating their preferences or looking beyond the usual suspects. 

These days, “people are more curious and willing to experiment,” he says. “The curiosity goes across generations. There’s a gravitation at all levels and at all ages for people to understand a bit about what they’re drinking and get excited about different things.” 

Chase Sinzer agrees. The owner of Claud, Stars, and Penny in New York City has observed a sea change in the ways people approach wine lists. In the 2010s, guests at restaurants where he worked would come in and say, “‘I know what I want, and it’s going to be Bordeaux or Brunello, and I’d like to spend this amount of money, and I don’t want anyone to talk to me,’” he recalls. “That same person now goes, ‘Can you please give me a few options? I can’t wait to hear what you have to say.’”

Ritchie links some of the open-mindedness and exploratory zeal to the effects of the pandemic. During shutdowns, many people studied wine. When hospitality businesses reopened, they shed their sweatpants, went out to bars and restaurants, and were eager to taste everything that the wide world of wine had to offer. Like their customers, retailers experienced these discovery trends, too.

Better, Not More

This same time period coincided with an enduring emphasis on moderation over excess. “Everyone is drinking less, for health reasons or generally for interest in living a more balanced life,” says Ritchie. 

That’s not a death knell, either. It’s a call to action. When someone is more knowledgeable and curious about what they drink, they can investigate each purchase to tailor it to their tastes and budgets. These are prime conditions to create lasting relationships with wine—ones with more long-term benefits than intermittent, happy-hour binges.

This all presents an opportunity for sommeliers, salespeople, and other wine professionals to meet people where they are and cultivate their curiosity. It’s a chance to learn from and avoid the knee-jerk anti-Merlot or Anything But Chardonnay sentiments of previous eras that led many folks to write off entire categories or wine itself without a second thought (or glass). “We’re making up for previous sins of sommeliers of different generations now,” Sinzer says.  

Besides, in the current economic moment, few of us are sitting on mountains of surplus cash to throw at lackluster wine. Trading multiple mediocre glasses for something you really love aligns with the way many people spend. They might be willing to shell out a few extra dollars for one great glass or bottle from a producer who shares their values, if consumer behaviors in fair-trade coffee, organic produce, and thrifted versus fast fashion are any indication.  

A quality-over-quantity mindset creates new and better points of access to wine, Liu says. “People are willing to spend $15 on something good and only have one bottle that night, rather than spend $15 on a case of poorly made beverages without thinking about it,” he says. “That’s actually helping the industry in a lot of ways because you have a new entry to the market that’s not garbage.”

Meaningful change takes time, and many grape growers, winemakers, and retailers need the market to rebound yesterday. But wine is a long game, too. After 8,000 years, how we think about, make, and drink it continues to evolve. Even if you only have one pour on any given night, that glass is still half-full.
